cues.txt: Welcome back to Jobster Stories. [music]
Last episode, we talked about the skills
you already have. This episode, we're
going to talk about how you use those
skills to future-proof your career. I'm
Jen, a career coach, [music] and your
go-to gal for all things career advice.
>> And I'm Priya. We've got your back as
you take on the wild [music] ride of job
hunting. Welcome to Jobster Stories.
>> Donna Bungard from Indeed is back with
[music] us to give us all the tips.
Donna, let's get into it. Everyone's
talking about AI taking jobs, but
Indeed's data shows something truly
surprising. Human skills are actually in
higher demand than ever. So, tell us,
what's really going on?
>> At a time of AI, we're seeing that a lot
of mundane tasks are being automated.
What people are also finding is that how
we talk to each other is becoming more
important. How we teach computers to
talk in our voice is becoming important.
How we interact and organize and do all
the things around it is important,
because frankly, everything is moving
faster, which means we need to be better
at those business operation skills that
we see across so many industries in
their job description. They're now
needing people to come in and be human
while they let the machines be the
machines.
>> Donna, you said human skills are more
valuable than ever, but the advice I
keep hearing is upskill, reskill,
reskill, upskill. For someone who's
feeling overwhelmed by that, where do
you even start?
>> That's a really good question, and the
truth of the matter is, we're always
upskilling. I can't imagine the skills I
have now that I had 15 years ago. What's
happening now is that everybody is
feeling the pressure to upskill at once,
which is where a lot of this
overwhelming piece comes from. We are
constantly evolving as professionals, as
people. That's supposed to happen. We're
We're growing constantly. It's the idea
that everybody in every system all over
around us is changing at once that's
where it gets scary. To help combat
that, couple things first, just take a
beat and acknowledge the fact that it's
not that you lack the skills. It is that
what we're doing and how work is getting
done is changing very, very quickly. And
you do have skills that are applicable
to this. However, we're going to need to
maybe approach them differently or apply
them slightly differently. And that's
okay. And that's a lot less scary than
saying I need to completely reskill. You
just need to focus your evolution and
your continual growth in a area that's
going to be adaptable.
>> Thank you for bringing up that
everyone's upskilling and everyone has
to keep learning. I have to say for
myself coming from within Indeed sales
to R&D to marketing, in each new
department, I thought, well, these
people have been in this department for
years. They just have it all covered.
But you learn that to your point,
everyone's having to upskill and reskill
constantly. So, you're not necessarily
behind. You may bring different skills
that others don't have and then you have
to learn some skills that they have in
addition to the skills that are becoming
more relevant. So, thank you for
touching on that because I think it's
important for job seekers to hear that.
And I think also that you don't have to
upskill in 18 areas all at once. Keep it
simple. Like that resonated with me a
lot, Donna. But I think the real reason
most people don't make a move is not
that they don't have the skills, but
that they don't believe in themselves.
So, how do they get past that?
>> There's a couple of ways to do it. I
have been known to say that because of
my age, Gen Xer, it's usually a matter
of, well, we do it first and then we
worry about it after. And I'm not sure I
can speak for an entire generation, but
I can say growing up in New England, we
tended to have that kind of you got to
go for it. But there's a reason why that
saying that fake it till you make it or
whatever is everywhere also. We don't
always believe in ourselves, but if you
know you can do really close, maybe you
can learn the rest on the job and just
be honest, be transparent, but don't
sell yourself short. At the end of the
day, nobody's ever a perfect fit that
checks every box. On our last episode,
we talked about how the skills in a job
description are wish list, not a
checklist, and it comes down to that
understanding that we don't need to
check every box. We have value and we
bring value, and as long as you're
willing to be adaptable and keep
learning, that value in many situations
can translate. Now, I'm not going to say
if anyone should ever put me in an
operating room. I don't have those
skills, but at the same time, so many of
my skills translate in so many different
places, and I'm just one person. We have
billions of people out there with a
billions and billions of skills, and
nobody's ever just one thing.
>> Absolutely. That imposter syndrome is
real at every level.
>> Oh, it's awful.
>> Donna, there's growing recognition that
people who are neurodivergent may
approach work differently. How should
employers and job seekers think about
neurodiversity as a source of valuable
skills and strengths rather than
something that needs to be overcome?
>> I think having Germa a disability
advocate said it best is people don't
overcome their disability. They're still
disabled at the end of the day. I am
mysteriously neurodivergent. We all
think a little differently. We all have
our different life experiences and such,
and people who are neurodivergent just
tend to think in somewhat different
patterns, but the first thing to note is
that no two people are ever going to be
the same. So, how this mysterious
neurodivergence presents and somebody
else who is in their late 40s, female
identifying, and probably ADHD presents
are going to be very, very different
because we are different human beings.
That said, my ability to switch gears,
get really curious, and dive in deep,
ramp up quickly, and just work with
things like that. Huge skill sets
because of the way I think. I have a
gentleman in my in my personal circle
who is ADHD and autistic, who his
ability to hyperfocus and become an
expert on a topic of interest is a huge
asset. It is also his ability to look at
a situation and automatically play
through the scenarios in his head in an
instant and come up with the best piece.
The way he communicates it might be a
little different than the way I will be,
but it is a direct, clear style of
communication that is highly effective.
So, what happens is sometimes these
communication styles are considered my
case less focused, in his overly direct,
we're actually both highly effective
communicators. We just aren't
necessarily drumming to the same beat as
everyone else. So, what I always try to
do is showcase how I'm going to play
into my strengths. I'm going to join the
field of technology where I have 50
slacks, 200 emails, and a bunch of
things to keep me interested all the
time in all of these different spaces.
He is picking a field that is highly
mathematical and orderly because that
works
for his way of thinking. The challenge
isn't whether or not somebody's
neurodivergent. The challenge is are the
employers prepared to understand the
different ways of communicating? Are
they prepared to realize that I'm
talking a lot, but it doesn't mean I'm
not paying attention either. I I'm
pretty good at reading a room. We need
to be able to understand that getting to
know the person and their strengths,
just because they may communicate or
work in different patterns, it doesn't
mean it's less effective, and it comes
down to can I get the job done, not how
am I getting the job done, and what
strengths do I have are going to balance
out weaknesses someone else on the team
has, and how is that collaboration going
to produce results?
>> You did a really great job of tying that
back to what we're talking about, right?
Which is is skills-based hiring, that
there are neurodivergent candidates that
bring so much to the table and can
really round out a team. And it's really
interesting now with the newer ways that
we're seeing employers do first rounds
of interviews or second rounds of
interviews. And that in some cases you
can record the video answers. And for
some that's more difficult, but maybe
for a neurodivergent candidate that
gives them the time and space they need
to be able to show their true skills in
a video. And so we need to think about
these candidates, not only how effective
they can be in the workforce, but how
we're approaching their interview
process to ensure that we can get a
really full picture of what it is that
they bring to the table. So Donna, if
someone's thinking about a career
transition, say a teacher moving into
corporate training or project
management, how do they figure out which
of their skills actually transfer over?
>> That's a really interesting question. I
think it comes down to the idea that
it's not necessarily where you perform
the position as you have the scheduling.
You have understanding educational
processes. You have an understanding of
different ways of thinking and learning.
You have all of those individual skills.
And it might come down to looking at a
few different job descriptions and
seeing how a corporate environment
approaches that a little bit differently
than say a K-12 environment. They might
talk about that scheduling as an agenda
setting or a day scheduling or something
like that. Look at what those keywords
are and just kind of translate them into
the industry. So it's just a little bit
of homework and kind of a flexible
thinking about not was I a teacher, but
what did I actually do and how did I
think about the work.
>> Such a good point. What did I actually
do and how do I think about the work?
With AI tools becoming part of almost
every job, what does human value
actually mean in an interview in 2026?
So, how do you really show that?
>> There's a lot of experts out there who
are defining it differently, and I've
read that several books on it, and at
the end of the day, human value is
what's going to make people connect to
the work you're producing. However that
shows up, whether it be in that
communication, in that adaptability, in
the facilitation, the teaching, any of
these things. How it all is going to be
different, but the human value is going
to be how others connect to the work.
How are people empowered by the work?
And seeing themselves reflected in your
product or services.
>> It's really important to remember that
there's always going to be a human side.
And so, we just have to, to your point,
it's going to be different for every
role and every industry, and just
connecting the dots is really important.
Donna, if you had one piece of advice
that you could give to someone who wants
to future-proof their career, not just
for their next job, but for the next
decade, what would it be?
>> I would start looking at your skills you
have differently, kind of take a bit of
an audit, and then look at where you
want to go, where can you be flexible,
how do you learn best, and pick one
thing, one thing that's going to help
you on that next step, and choose that,
knowing that what you choose to learn
now does not have to define the next 20
years of your life, but it's going to
help you take the path and get you set
up for that constantly learning piece.
>> Absolutely. I think you mentioned it
yourself, Donna, with your career, and I
can attest to the same, that you stayed
curious, right? It wasn't a linear path
for you. It was like, "Oh, this sounds
interesting." You stayed curious, and
then you said you had the grit and and
the confidence to say, "I'm just going
to do it," and then you figured out
where the skills were. And then that's
pretty impressive. Maybe we should
follow your path, Donna. Have you
written a book yet, Donna?
>> Oh gosh, no. And please follow your own
path. Mine is a comedy of errors, but
everyone's is. That's something also to
know if you're looking back. And as much
as I joke about my comedy of errors, I
look back and think, "Oh, I should have
done that differently." We all do. I
learn something, and I learn something
through that. I don't call it grit, I
call it being stubborn. You just got to
be more stubborn than the process.
>> That's absolutely right. My kids are
definitely more stubborn than any
process I put in place.
>> So, oh yeah.
>> Yeah, same. Same.
>> Anyways, Donna, this has been incredibly
useful for anyone thinking about where
work is heading and what they need to do
to get there. I really can't thank you
enough. You are always one of my
favorite people to talk to, and I hope
we can do this again. For more expert
tips on how to navigate your career, be
sure to subscribe to Indeed's [music]
YouTube channel, and follow Job Search
Stories wherever you listen to podcasts.
Thanks for listening to Job Search
Stories, and we'll [music] see you next
time.
